title: Which Otto Engine Is the Fastest?
authors: Idriss Hank Nkouatchoua Ngueya, Marcin Łobejko
abstract: A general thermal machine is characterized by distinct time or energy scales: temperature, coupling to the heat baths, internal free dynamics and interactions, and external driving. We address the question: what parameters determine the speed of a given engine, and how can they be used to reliably compare different types of engine? Specifically, we consider four realizations of the Otto engine, each operating with the same Otto efficiency, and aim to characterize and compare their power outputs. The main insight of this paper is that, irrespective of their very different dynamical implementations, the power of each engine can be factorized into a common characteristic work and an implementation-specific characteristic time. The characteristic work depends only on the internal frequencies of the machine and the temperatures, whereas the characteristic time depends on the coupling strength to the baths and on the implementation-specific driving. This observation allows us to compare the power of different engines through their characteristic times and thereby reduce the relevant parameter space to parameters that capture the dynamical aspects of engine performance. Despite different dynamical implementations, this framework reveals simple common features. In all cases, the maximum operating speed is limited by a common timescale given by the sum of the characteristic thermalization times of the hot and cold baths. Moreover, the four engines fall into two distinct asymptotic classes: implementations in which driving and thermalization occur simultaneously exhibit quadratic scaling, whereas those in which work extraction and thermalization alternate exhibit linear scaling. These results expose general dynamical features that determine the operational speed of quantum Otto engines.
summary: This paper develops a general theory to compare the performance of various quantum Otto engines by factoring the power into a work term and an implementation-specific time scale. It demonstrates that the maximum operating speed is fundamentally limited by the thermalization times of the hot and cold baths, regardless of the specific cycle used.
main_problem: The paper aims to systematically compare the operational speed (power output) of different quantum realizations of the Otto engine, despite them achieving the same thermodynamic efficiency.
main_result: The power of any quantum Otto engine can be factorized into a characteristic work (dependent on internal frequencies) and an implementation-specific characteristic time. The maximum speed is universally limited by the sum of the hot and cold bath thermalization times.
method: The analysis uses a factorization approach ($P = W/T^*$) to separate thermodynamic and dynamical aspects, comparing four distinct dynamical realizations (e.g., four-stroke, always-on, Floquet-modulated).
model_or_system: The system is a quantum heat engine, modeled using qubits coupled to thermal baths, analyzed via master equations and Hamiltonian dynamics for various cycle implementations.
key_observables: Power output ($P$), characteristic work ($W$), characteristic time ($T^*$), and efficiency ($\eta$).
important_parameters: Coupling strengths ($	au, \Omega$), internal frequencies ($\omega$), and dimensionless ratios characterizing the cycle dynamics ($s_{LT}, s_F, s_\pi$).
main_assumptions: The core assumption is the factorization $P = W/T^*$, allowing the comparison to focus solely on the characteristic time $T^*$. Various approximations are used depending on the cycle (e.g., slow modulation, fast oscillation limit).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the four-stroke model and the Floquet-inspired model for a single qubit, and the two-qubit realization, comparing power scaling in different regimes.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the general framework by factorizing power, then analyzes specific dynamical realizations (four-stroke, Floquet, always-on, on-off) by deriving their respective characteristic times and asymptotic scaling laws.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, general framework for comparing non-equilibrium quantum processes, showing how fundamental thermodynamic limits constrain the speed achievable by different physical implementations.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The figures illustrate a quantum Otto engine based on a single qubit serving as the working medium and subject to an external time-dependent drive. Panel (a) depicts the conventional four-stroke realization, where the qubit frequency is modulated between two values through a sequence of expansion and compression strokes. In this case, the frequency varies linearly within each stroke. Panel (b) presents a Floquet-inspired realization in which the qubit frequency undergoes a continuous periodic modulation, with a driving period shorter than the characteristic relaxation timescale of the system.

Figure 2: The figures above illustrate a quantum Otto engine based on two interacting qubits serving as the working medium and coupled to independent hot and cold thermal reservoirs. The qubits interact through an externally controlled transverse coupling. Panel (a) depicts the always-on realization, where the coupling remains active throughout the operation and the qubit frequencies undergo continuous periodic modulation. Panel (b) presents the on-off realization, in which the interaction is periodically switched on and off, generating a sequence of discrete work strokes separated by thermalization stages.

Figure 3: Normalized characteristic operational times for the always-on and Floquet implementations as functions of their respective dimensionless control parameters. The blue curve shows the always-on result, S∗ always−on = 1 + s2 π/π2, while the red curve shows S∗ Floquet = J−2 1 (s−1 F ). The orange dashed line denotes the large-sF Floquet asymptote 1 + 4s2 F . The nonmonotonic behavior and divergences of the Floquet curve at small sF are discussed in the main text. Since sπ and sF have different physical definitions, the figure compares their scaling behavior rather than their performance at fixed experimental resources.

Figure 4: Optimized normalized characteristic operational times of the four-stroke (solid curves) and on-off (dashed curves) implementations. The upper panel shows their dependence on the model-specific operation parameter for κ = 1, 0.1, and 0.01. The lower panel shows their dependence on the relaxation-time asymmetry κ for fixed operation parameters s = 1, 10, and 100. Here κ = 1 corresponds to equal relaxation times, whereas κ →0 denotes the strongly asymmetric limit. Both implementations exhibit asymptotically linear growth with leading slope κ/2.

Figure 5: Ratio R = S∗ on−off(sπ, κ)/S∗ always−on(sπ) as a function of the common operation parameter sπ for different values of the relaxation-time asymmetry κ. The line R = 1 (dashed) separates the regimes in which the always-on (R > 1) and on-off (R < 1) implementations have the shorter characteristic operational time.
